intro: Wet room installations in Borthwickterrace have grown steadily in demand over recent years, and it's easy to see why. Whether you're adapting a bathroom for accessibility, modernising an older property, or simply wanting a sleek, open shower space, a well-designed wet room can transform one of your most-used rooms. Borthwickterrace's mix of period homes and newer builds means every project comes with its own set of challenges and opportunities. Getting the right installer — someone who understands the local construction styles and knows what's under those older floors — makes all the difference between a wet room that lasts decades and one that causes damp problems within a few years.
localContext: Borthwickterrace sits in Midlothian and is characterised by a range of property types that each present distinct considerations for wet room work. The older stone-built properties and period cottages common in the area often have solid stone or timber suspended floors with little tolerance for error when it comes to waterproofing and drainage falls. Stone walls can also hold moisture, so the tanking and membrane work needs to be thorough and appropriate for the substrate. Modern estate homes in Borthwickterrace tend to have more standard concrete or chipboard floors, which are somewhat easier to work with, though they still require careful preparation. Borthwickterrace sits in a moderately hard water area, which is worth factoring in when choosing fixtures and finishes — limescale can build up on glass screens and chrome fittings over time, so specifying easy-clean coatings or matte finishes tends to pay off in the long run. A good installer will discuss this with you upfront rather than leaving you to discover it six months later.
serviceDetail: A proper wet room installation in Borthwickterrace follows a clear sequence of work that, when done properly, takes most properties between four and seven working days depending on size and complexity. The process starts with a survey visit, where the installer assesses the floor construction, existing drainage, water supply routes, and the condition of walls and subfloor. This is especially important in the older cottages around Borthwickterrace, where unexpected timber rot or uneven stone floors can add time and cost if not identified early. Once the survey is complete and a design agreed, the first physical stage is stripping out the existing bathroom, removing sanitaryware, tiles, and often the floor covering itself. The subfloor is then assessed and, if needed, built up or levelled before a linear or central drain is positioned to achieve the correct gradient — typically around 1:80 fall toward the outlet. The entire floor and lower walls are then tanked using a liquid waterproof membrane, applied in multiple coats, with reinforcing tape at joints. This stage is non-negotiable and is where poor installations cut corners. Wall boarding or tile adhesion follows, then tiling or alternative wall finishes, before sanitaryware, a thermostatic shower valve, and any glass or frameless screen elements are fitted. Final sign-off should include checking every seal, running the shower for an extended period, and confirming drainage is clear.
pricing: Wet room installations in Borthwickterrace typically fall between £6,000 and £12,000 for a full conversion, though the actual cost depends heavily on the size of the room, the property type, and your choice of finishes. A straightforward wet room in a modern estate home will sit at the lower end of that range. In an older stone-built cottage or period property, where floor levels may need significant work and tanking demands more preparation, costs often reach £9,000 to £12,000. High-end tiling, bespoke glass screens, or underfloor heating all push the price upward. Always get an itemised quote so you can see exactly what's included — especially the waterproofing specification.
whyLocal: Choosing a tradesperson who has worked in and around Borthwickterrace matters more than it might seem. Local installers will have hands-on experience with the type of construction common here — they'll know how older Midlothian stone properties behave, where to expect awkward floor joist layouts, and how to route new drainage without unnecessary disruption to period features. They're also easier to hold accountable if anything needs attention after the job is done. A wet room is a significant investment, and having someone who is familiar with Borthwickterrace properties specifically — not just generic bathroom fitting — gives you real confidence in the finished result.

faqs.q: Can a wet room be installed in an older stone-built cottage in Borthwickterrace?
faqs.a: Yes, but it requires more careful preparation than a modern home. Stone floors and walls need thorough tanking with appropriate membranes, and the floor may need levelling work before the drainage fall can be set correctly. An experienced installer will survey the property first to flag any structural considerations specific to older Borthwickterrace homes before any work begins.

faqs.q: How does the moderately hard water in Borthwickterrace affect my wet room?
faqs.a: Hard water causes limescale to build up on glass screens, chrome fittings, and tile grout over time. In Borthwickterrace, it's worth specifying easy-clean glass coatings and considering matte or brushed finishes on brassware, which show deposits less readily. A water softener fitted to the incoming supply can also extend the life and appearance of your wet room significantly.

faqs.q: How long does a wet room installation take in Borthwickterrace?
faqs.a: Most standard wet room projects take between four and seven working days on site. Older properties in Borthwickterrace can occasionally take longer if the survey reveals issues like uneven subfloors, concealed pipework that needs re-routing, or timber that requires treatment before waterproofing can begin. Your installer should give you a realistic programme after the initial survey visit.

faqs.q: Is planning permission needed for a wet room conversion in Borthwickterrace?
faqs.a: In most cases, no — wet room conversions are considered internal alterations and don't require planning permission. However, if your Borthwickterrace property is a listed building or sits within a conservation area, you should check with Midlothian Council before work starts. A good local installer will be able to advise you on this as part of the initial consultation.
